pillar_reactions.evidence: Pre-sold on the modality and articulating the benefit himself before the pillar was presented: "what I like about kettlebells is that it's not fixed on one position, it's actually a lot to do with movement, and it works a lot on the joints... you don't need that many equipment and instruments, and you can do at home, which is very important for me." When the rep tied it to soccer he finished the thought unprompted — rep: "when you're running down the line, you'd be like, I can run for longer" — prospect: "Or the, the changes in the movement. Yeah." Mobility was one of his two stated success criteria.

He engaged on mechanics rather than accepting or objecting, and raised the one thing that worried him twice: "problem with fasting, I know that it doesn't only burn fat, but also muscle, so I have to be careful with that" and then "But is it true that it consumes some muscles as well?" The rep answered from personal practice ("I fast 36 hours once a week and I'm pretty good with it") and closed it with "I won't worry about that too much". Prospect accepted the answer — "Cool" — but the concern was resolved by assertion rather than evidence.

No enthusiasm and no resistance — he interrogated the operating model against his own diary. "Stupid question, but what happens if a week I miss two out of four trainings?" and "Trevor is based, which time zone?" Both answered satisfactorily (pause the programme and credit the week; California/Pacific, so evenings his time) and he closed the section with "It's clear on the process." Notable given that having never been coached was the root cause he himself ranked number one — the pillar aimed squarely at his gap drew only procedural questions, because the rep never connected the two.

anchors.raw: haven't been followed by a tutor. So I've been always auto-didact online researching. So probably that has put an impediment to the progress as well.
anchors.note: His incumbent is free and he has used it for years. He also framed it as the thing that has held him back, which converts the anchor from a price objection into a reason to buy — the rep noted it in passing ("if you get a coach that solves the other problem") but never priced the cost of the years lost to it.

anchors.raw: I allocate two to three hours a week to playing squash. That's two times a week. And more than five, six hours a week playing soccer.
anchors.note: He already commits eight-plus hours a week to physical activity with club fees, kit and a Sunday league. Someone spending that much time is not arguing about whether fitness is worth money — and indeed he never questioned the $6,000, only the payment structure and the timing. Logged because it explains the absence of a price objection on a call where price was never defended.

unmet_demand.want: Kettlebell coaching for his wife — an athletic pilates and yoga practitioner
unmet_demand.why_unmet: He raised it himself and parked it — "by the way I'll have a follow-up question, is that recommended for women as well, kettlebells? but we can get back to that" — and neither party ever returned to it. Nothing in the offer as presented speaks to whether the programme takes women, whether there is a partner arrangement, or what it would cost. Almost certainly served by the product; simply never said.

unmet_demand.want: A programme that can absorb a heavy, unpredictable travel schedule and a year-long IPO process without being wasted
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Partially served and partially unsaid. The rep described pausing and week credits when asked about missed sessions, but never re-offered it against the actual objection, and the terms were vague ("we can pause the program and you just get the week back if needs be") with nothing about how long a programme can be paused or how that interacts with the six-month clock. The prospect's stated reservation — "I don't want to start and pause it" — is precisely the thing the policy answers.
